name: Monlunabant
lead: Monlunabant (also INV-202, MRI-1891) is an investigational, peripherally selective cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) inverse agonist developed for obesity and metabolic disease. It was discovered by researchers at the US National Institutes of Health and developed by Inversago Pharma, and is now associated with Novo Nordisk.[1] It is not approved for any use.

It belongs to a class whose first member, rimonabant, was approved in Europe in 2006 and withdrawn in 2008-2009 over psychiatric adverse events. Monlunabant was designed to act mostly outside the brain to reduce such effects.[1][2] A Phase 2a trial in adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome reported weight loss described as modest, together with mild to moderate neuropsychiatric effects such as anxiety and sleep disturbance; suicidal ideation was not reported.[1][3]

paras: Monlunabant blocks the CB1 receptor, which is involved in appetite and metabolism. Its designers aimed for peripheral selectivity, but a 2025 study titled as showing that it suppresses appetite through a central mechanism indicates that central effects remain relevant.[1][4]

A 16-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging Phase 2a trial at 25 Canadian sites evaluated monlunabant in adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome.[3] Secondary summaries describe modest weight loss and higher rates of mild to moderate neuropsychiatric events than placebo.[1] An open-label extension was published in 2026.[5] A Phase 2 trial in adults with diabetic kidney disease was also published in 2026.[6] A Phase 1 study in healthy Japanese and Caucasian men examined safety and blood concentrations after one dose.[7]

Rimonabant, the first CB1 inverse agonist, was approved by the European Commission in 2006 and withdrawn from the market in 2008-2009 after depressive disorders, anxiety and suicidal ideation were reported; the FDA never approved it.[2] Later peripherally restricted CB1 blockers, including monlunabant, have been developed in response, and a 2026 review discusses their potential in obesity and metabolic disease.[1][8]

card.summary: An experimental oral CB1 blocker for weight loss that showed modest results and some neuropsychiatric side effects in Phase 2.
card.note: Investigational; same drug class as rimonabant, withdrawn over psychiatric effects.

quick.overview:
Monlunabant is an experimental pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to reduce appetite and improve metabolism. It was designed to work mostly outside the brain.

A 16-week Phase 2a trial reported modest weight loss, and it is not approved anywhere.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor tied to appetite and energy balance. A 2025 study suggests part of its appetite effect is central.
quick.risks: The Phase 2a trial reported higher rates of mild to moderate anxiety and sleep disturbance than placebo; suicidal ideation was not reported. The earlier drug in this class, rimonabant, was withdrawn over psychiatric effects.
